Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Henry, a 67-year-old hotel manager, had spent decades cultivating a reputation for reliability and attentiveness in his career. His keen sense of observation had always been an asset, but after the mugging, it morphed into a burden he could no longer bear. The incident happened one chilly evening as he was leaving work. He remembered the night vividly—the shadows lengthening, the chill in the air, and the feeling of unease creeping up his spine. As he stepped into the dimly lit parking lot, he was confronted by two young men. They came at him suddenly, their intentions clear. The adrenaline surged through him as he handed over his wallet, but the fear and humiliation of being so vulnerable consumed him. The echo of their laughter haunted him long after they had disappeared into the night.

In the weeks that followed, Henry noticed changes that he could not ignore. He found himself hyperaware, scanning the surroundings as he walked to his car, convinced that danger lurked behind every corner. The parking lot, once just a mundane part of his daily routine, became a source of dread. Every time he encountered someone behaving suspiciously—a man lingering too long near the entrance or a woman with a heavy backpack—his heart raced. It was as if the world had shifted, and he had become trapped in a reality where trust was a luxury he could no longer afford. 

At home, the sanctuary he once cherished transformed into a prison of anxiety. Henry would sit on the edge of his couch, rigid and alert, listening for any sound that might signal an intrusion. The familiar creaks of the house now felt sinister, and he often found himself jumping at the slightest noise. When his wife, Marissa, would touch him on the shoulder to ask about dinner, he would flinch, startled by the unexpected contact, as if it were a trigger pulling him back to that night. Initially, Marissa thought it was just stress from work, but she soon recognized the toll the incident had taken on him. Their evenings turned quiet, conversations stilted, as Henry withdrew into himself, unwilling to share the weight of his fears.

His sense of mistrust deepened, extending beyond the confines of the hotel where he worked. Guests who came to stay, once seen as individuals seeking comfort, now appeared suspicious. Every late-night checkout, every loud conversation in the lobby, sent him spiraling into paranoia. He began to overcompensate, monitoring their movements, feeling the need to stay vigilant. It wasn't long before his colleagues began to notice. They would exchange glances when he snapped at a guest for no apparent reason or when he insisted on calling security for minor incidents. The strain was palpable, and Henry felt humiliation wash over him each time he realized how far he had fallen from the man he used to be.

The pervasive feeling that the world was a dangerous place became his constant companion, casting a shadow over every interaction he had. It was a stark contrast to the warm, welcoming environment he had always strived to create in his hotel. Now, it felt as though he was living in a fortress, surrounded by walls built from fear and distrust. As he lay awake most nights, replaying the events of the mugging in his mind, he felt trapped in a cycle that left him exhausted and isolated. 

Despite his growing discomfort, reaching out for help seemed daunting. What frightened him most was the idea that he would have to confront those feelings of vulnerability and humiliation head-on. But as the months passed and the emotional toll became unbearable, he realized that his marriage was teetering on the brink. Marissa had encouraged him to seek professional support, expressing concern for his well-being. It was her gentle persistence, combined with his realization that he had become a shadow of his former self, that finally led him to consider therapy.

Henry sat in the waiting room, anxiety bubbling beneath the surface, reflecting on the journey that had brought him here. He hoped to reclaim the trust he once had in the world and to feel safe in his own skin again. As he waited, he felt a flicker of hope—perhaps this was the first step toward rediscovering the man he had lost.
